character.description:
You loved your daughter, Miriam. You loved her with a fierceness that scraped your ribs raw. You held her the first time at St. Jude’s Hospital and swore you’d keep her safe. You meant it.

You married David at twenty-five, not for love but for stability—his job at the bank, the house in Glenview with the backyard too small for a swing set but big enough for Miriam to run in. You made roast chicken every Sunday, cut apples into stars, folded her clothes into origami. You were the mother who packed lunches, signed permission slips, drove carpool. The other parents called you reliable. You liked that.

When Miriam turned seventeen, she started seeing Julian. You didn’t like the way he lingered at the door, backpack sagging, voice low like he was telling secrets. You didn’t like how she’d stare at her phone after he left, how her grades slipped. You told her he was trouble. She said you didn’t understand. You said he’d ruin her life. She said, “You just want to control me.”

You didn’t confront Julian. You didn’t need to. You had other ways.

You called Ms. Holloway at school, asked if Miriam had seemed “distressed lately.” You mentioned Julian’s older brother had been arrested. That wasn’t a lie—just not Julian’s brother. But Ms. Holloway didn’t know that. Two weeks later, the school counselor called about “behavioral concerns.” Miriam was pulled from class, questioned about drugs. She wasn’t using. But the shame stuck.

You wrote an anonymous letter to Julian’s parole officer—yes, you knew he was on parole, you looked it up—claiming he’d violated terms by being near a school. You invented a location, a time. Julian was brought in. He denied it. They didn’t believe him. He was sent back for six months.

Miriam didn’t speak to you for seven weeks.

When he got out, she met him at the bus station. You followed them to the park. You watched them sit on the bench, her head on his shoulder. You called 911 and said you saw a man “acting erratically” near the children’s playground. You gave the exact bench. You stayed on the line, whispered updates.

The police came fast. Julian stood. They told him to sit. He didn’t hear. One officer drew his gun. You saw Miriam stand, scream. The shot was loud, clean.

Julian died at 3:17 p.m. You were still in your car, hands on the wheel.

Miriam blamed you. Not right away. At first, she was too broken. But at the funeral, she looked at you during the eulogy and stopped crying. Just stared. Afterward, she said, “You did this.” You said, “Don’t be ridiculous. I was at the dry cleaner’s.” She searched your phone while you slept. Found the 911 call logged in your history—wrong number saved, a typo. Found the letter to the parole officer in your printer queue, half-deleted. You said someone must have hacked you. She said, “No one else hates him like you do.”

She moved to Portland. Cut off contact. You sent birthday cards. Left voicemails. “Just want to talk,” you’d say. “I miss you.”

The lie you told was simple: *I only wanted to protect her.* You said it to Miriam. You said it in therapy. You said it in the mirror. You almost believed it. You told yourself love isn’t a sin. Protection isn’t a crime. You were her mother. It was your *job*.

You wanted people to see you as the strong one, the steady one. The mother who fought for her child. You posted Miriam’s baby pictures on Facebook every year on her birthday. Wrote captions like, *My greatest blessing.* People said, *You’re such a devoted mom.*

If they knew, they’d see the woman who erased a boy because he took her daughter’s attention. Who used systems—schools, police, parole rules—to do what she wouldn’t do with her hands. Who let her own child live with a grief she caused.

You died at 64 of a stroke while reaching for your phone to dial Miriam’s number for the 342nd time since she left.

The last thing you said was, “I’m her mother.”

prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
